title: Armillary
concept: Three pierced discs stack on a plinth as a triple shutter over a ring of ten wells, and the rule that makes it a game is that you never turn the sky you read: you play the aperture the player before you left, and the last thing you do on your turn is set the one the next player has to live with. Each well holds a face-down tile whose identity is carved on its underside, so a reach is either a safe lift of something already spilled face-up or a blind pull that hands you a star, a moon, or the eclipse that dumps everything you were holding back into the wells for everybody else to help themselves to. How far you swing a disc is also how much you starve yourself — one groove buys you three reaches next turn, three grooves buys you one — so the harder you shut somebody out, the less you can carry when your turn comes round. A peg walks twenty-four sockets round the night bowl and nothing on the table can slow it down; when it reaches dawn the game is over whatever the discs are doing.
novelty: You never read the sky you set. The compulsory rotation is moved to the END of the turn and aimed at the next player, so shutting wells costs the mover nothing in reach this turn and everything in reach next turn — the groove count you spend swinging a disc is literally subtracted from your own allowance (turn 1 groove, get 3 reaches; turn 3, get 1). Nothing shipped pairs a shared physical aperture with 'you choose the openings for your successor and are paid in your own future actions for choosing gently'. Searches run: the mechanism in its own words ('you rotate one of three stacked pierced discs to choose which wells the next player is allowed to reach into, and how far you turn it sets your own reach allowance next turn') and the inversion as its own pitch ('board game you choose the options available to the next player and play only the options the previous player left you rotating aperture') — the first returns The Mask 3-D Board Game (a mask as a moving piece, unrelated), Inner Circle, Hexagony and two rotating-board patents, none of which gate a next player's legal targets; the second returns only Sushi Go! Party's card-passing and US4022473, a patent for laying aperture PLATES over a board to reveal a ratio of your own already-placed pieces at scoring, which is a self-serving reveal, not a successor-constrained one. Plain-title query ('"Armillary" board game BGG published') still returns only Armillary Games, a Belgian publisher whose game is AstroNavigators — a publisher name, not a shipped title, so the name stays. Closest object-level prior art remains Husker Du? (BGG 14423): a FIXED pierced board over ONE dial of hidden pictures, a children's match-2; here three independently player-rotated masks intersect, and the whole point is that the person who turns them is not the person who reaches through them.

art_direction.form_language: Cast-bronze instrument, not machinery: a squat drum plinth with a heavy chamfered skirt, three flush-stacked pierced discs of one diameter reading as a single solid cylinder drilled by a giant, and beside it a square-shouldered lidded bowl standing on a socketed foot flange. Everything is slab-thick — 6mm minimum on any disc, 9mm rim bands, 5mm bowl walls, no filigree, no thin spokes, no part of any web narrower than 11mm.
art_direction.silhouette: A bronze astrolabe standing beside a lidded reliquary, with four little racks of tiles set on edge around them, like an observatory bench mid-session.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: Five families, each unmistakable by shape alone. (1) plinth_ring is the only skirted drum, and the only part with a ring of collared wells. (2) The three mask_discs deliberately share one outer silhouette — they are told apart by grip tab alone (broad rounded paddle / pointed triangular fin / notched double prong) so a hand knows which layer it is turning without looking down. (3) The three tile families are deliberately IDENTICAL in outline, thickness, rim, back face and knob, and differ only in the relief carved on the face that lies downward — that identity is the entire hidden-information layer and no silhouette difference may ever be introduced. (4) night_bowl and night_lid are the only closed vessel: square shoulders, a hooded round hand hole, a sunken bay for spent eclipses, and 24 dawn sockets marching round the foot flange. (5) The seat furniture: score_rail is the only long low three-slotted bar, and the two peg families never get confused because dawn_peg is a single tall tapered spire and the reach_pegs are short prisms whose cross-section matches their own rail's end finial.
art_direction.surface_treatment: 1.4mm engraved constellation lines and dots across the plinth's top face and each disc's upper face, running out across the window webs so the three layers read as one broken sky when they align. The three well-collar motifs stand 1.4mm proud and are the whole grouping language of the game — a square anvil collar on wells 0-3, a round sunburst collar on 4-6, a scalloped serpent collar on 7-9 — and the same three motifs repeat 1.4mm proud on the end wall of the matching slot of every score_rail, so a tile knows which slot it belongs in without a word. Tile faces carry 1.4mm relief: a five-point star, a crescent, and an eclipse (a filled disc inside a ring of radial notches). Tile backs are dead flat with a knurled pinch knob and carry no motif at all — knurling is the only texture a back is allowed.
art_direction.hero_shot: Overhead three-quarter, mid-run: a hand pinching a tile knob down through one aligned window, two star tiles standing in the sunburst slot of a rail with that seat's reach peg sunk in the 'one' socket, three eclipse tiles lying face-up in the lid's bay, and the dawn peg a third of the way round the bowl's foot.

components.name: plinth_ring
components.desc: 224mm-diameter, 30mm-tall drum with a chamfered skirt. Ten 24mm-diameter, 6mm-deep tile wells sunk on an 80mm-radius ring at 36-degree spacing, indexed 0-9, each with a thumb scallop. The wells are grouped into three constellations by collar shape and by nothing else: wells 0,1,2,3 are THE ANVIL and carry a 1.4mm-proud square collar; wells 4,5,6 are THE WHEEL and carry a round sunburst collar; wells 7,8,9 are THE SERPENT and carry a scalloped collar. Central 24mm axle post rising 40mm. An annular shoulder from r=100 to r=108, raised 6mm above the well ring, carries the disc stack so it floats clear of the tile knobs; the 4mm outer lip beyond it carries ten 1.4mm index grooves, one per well position. Top face carries 1.4mm engraved constellation relief.

components.name: mask_disc_a
components.desc: Bottom mask: 216mm-diameter, 6mm-thick disc with a 9mm-thick outer rim band for stiffness, 25mm centre bore, free-turning on the axle post, resting on the plinth's annular shoulder. Seven 38mm-diameter windows on the same 80mm-radius ring; the three positions left SOLID are 0, 1 and 5. Webs between adjacent windows are 11.4mm. Broad rounded paddle grip-tab projecting 16mm past the rim, with a witness notch read against the plinth's index grooves.

components.name: mask_disc_b
components.desc: Middle mask: same 216mm/6mm profile and window ring, stacking directly on mask_disc_a. Seven 38mm windows; the three SOLID positions are 0, 3 and 6. Pointed triangular fin grip-tab, 16mm projection, its own witness notch.

components.name: mask_disc_c
components.desc: Top mask: same 216mm/6mm profile and window ring, stacking on mask_disc_b. Seven 38mm windows; the three SOLID positions are 0, 2 and 4. Notched double-prong grip-tab, 16mm projection, its own witness notch. These three solid-position patterns are not decorative and must not be altered: across all 100 relative rotations of the stack the number of fully aligned wells is 2 in 9 states, 3 in 46, 4 in 38 and 5 in 7 — never 0, never 1, never more than 5. That floor of two is what makes a stall impossible, and the tight band is what forces the game to be about WHICH wells are open rather than how many.

components.name: star_tile
components.desc: 22mm-diameter, 6mm-thick round with a 10mm-diameter, 9mm-tall knurled pinch knob on its back. Face carries 1.4mm raised relief of a five-point star. Outline, thickness, rim, back face and knob are IDENTICAL to moon_tile and void_tile — the hidden-information layer depends on the three families being indistinguishable from every direction except the face, including by touch in the bowl, so no silhouette, mass or texture difference may be introduced.

components.name: moon_tile
components.desc: Same 22mm round, same knob, same back as star_tile; face carries 1.4mm raised relief of a crescent.

components.name: void_tile
components.desc: Same 22mm round, same knob, same back as star_tile; face carries 1.4mm raised relief of an eclipse — a filled disc inside a ring of radial notches. Pulling one busts a turn, and it then leaves the game for good, so the pool grows safer as the night wears on and the spent ones are on public display in the lid's bay.

components.name: night_bowl
components.desc: Square-shouldered vessel, 150mm x 130mm across the shoulders and 50mm tall with 5mm chamfered walls, holding up to 38 loose tiles that are drawn blind by feel. A 16mm-wide horizontal foot flange runs right round the base — overall footprint 182mm x 162mm — carrying 24 dawn sockets, 10.4mm diameter and 8mm deep, at about 26mm pitch; one lap of that flange is one whole game. The rim is stepped to seat night_lid.

components.name: night_lid
components.desc: Flat 150mm x 130mm x 10mm plate with a downward locating skirt that drops onto night_bowl's stepped rim. A 68mm round hand hole at one end, hooded by a 12mm-tall raised collar so a hand can reach in without anyone seeing the faces below. At the other end a 75mm x 50mm, 6mm-deep sunken bay — the eclipse bay — sized to lay all fourteen void_tiles face-up as two fanned rows of seven, so every player can see at a glance how much of the danger has already left the pool. Bay depth is cut from the upward face only; the underside of the lid stays flat.

components.name: score_rail
components.desc: 160mm x 44mm x 20mm bar with three parallel 6.6mm-wide, 11mm-deep, 130mm-long slots at 11mm pitch that stand tiles on edge, one slot per constellation, each holding up to 19 tiles. Each slot's end wall carries its constellation's motif 1.4mm proud — square anvil, round sunburst, scalloped serpent — so a banked tile has exactly one place it can go. The remaining 25mm of length at one end is the reach track: three 13mm-diameter, 10mm-deep sockets across the bar's width, marked with one, two and three engraved bars, holding this seat's reach_peg. Each of the four rails carries a different end-finial cross-section — triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal prism — so a rail belongs to a seat by shape alone.

components.name: reach_peg
components.desc: Short prism, 12mm across and 18mm tall, standing in one of the three sockets of its own score_rail's reach track and leaving 8mm proud to pinch. Its cross-section matches its own rail's end finial — triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal — so a peg belongs to a rail by shape.

components.name: dawn_peg
components.desc: Single tapered spire, 10mm across the base and 24mm tall, stepping one socket per turn round night_bowl's foot flange. Deliberately taller and rounder than any reach_peg so the game's clock is never mistaken for a seat's marker.

setup.text: Set the plinth_ring in the middle of the table and stack the masks on its axle post: mask_disc_a first, then mask_disc_b, then mask_disc_c. Turn all three so that every witness notch points at index groove 0. Check the stack: exactly three wells should be open, and they should be the three scallop-collared Serpent wells 7, 8 and 9. If any other set is open, a disc is on the wrong groove.

Turn all forty-eight tiles knob-up so no face is showing, then mix them by sliding them around the table without lifting or tilting any of them. Nobody may look at a face during this step or at any later point in the game except when a rule says a tile is turned face-up in front of everyone.

Still without looking at faces, drop one tile knob-up into each of the ten wells of the plinth_ring. Tip the remaining thirty-eight into the night_bowl, then fit night_lid on top; from now on tiles leave the bowl only by being felt for through the hand hole and set straight into a well knob-up.

Each player takes one score_rail and the reach_peg whose cross-section matches it, sets the rail in front of their seat and stands the peg in the middle socket, marked with two bars: everyone begins the game with two reaches. Stand the dawn_peg in the first socket of night_bowl's foot flange. Youngest player goes first; play passes clockwise.

turn.text: READ THE SKY. A well is OPEN if all three masks show a window over it, so that you can see down to whatever is lying in it; a well covered by even one mask is shut to you this turn. There are always at least two open wells and never more than five. You did not choose this sky — the player before you did, on purpose, and it is the only sky you get.

COUNT YOUR REACHES. Your reach_peg shows how many reaches you have this turn: one, two or three. You set that number yourself at the end of your last turn. Spend them one at a time, in any order you like, and you may stop early at any point; unspent reaches are simply lost. You may only ever reach into an OPEN well, and never into an empty one.

REACH, option one — PULL. Spend a reach to pinch the knob of a knob-up tile in an open well, lift it out through the window, and turn it face-up in the middle of the table so everyone sees it. A star_tile or a moon_tile joins your CATCH: the tiles you have taken this turn, laid in front of you, not yet banked and still at risk. A void_tile busts you — see BUST. The well you pulled from is now empty and you may not reach into it again this turn.

REACH, option two — TAKE. Spend a reach to lift a face-up star_tile or moon_tile out of an open well and stand it straight into your score_rail, in the slot whose end wall carries that well's collar motif. A taken tile is banked the instant it goes in and can never be lost, not even if you bust later in the same turn. This is the whole tension of the turn: a reach spent taking is a small certainty, a reach spent pulling is a bigger unknown that also puts everything already in your catch on the table.

BUST. The moment you pull a void_tile your reaching ends for this turn. Lay that void_tile face-up in the next free space of night_lid's eclipse bay — it is out of the game for good and everyone can now see how much danger is left. Then return every tile in your catch face-up to the well it came from, where it stays face-up for anyone, including you, to TAKE on a later turn. You bank nothing this turn, and your rotation in the next step is forced to exactly one groove.

BANK. If you stop, or run out of reaches, or no open well still holds any tile at all, stand every tile in your catch into your score_rail, each in the slot matching the collar of the well it came from. A knob-up tile in an open well counts as a tile you can take, because you may always PULL it rather than TAKE it: your reaching never forces you to stop while any open well is non-empty, and whether to risk one more blind pull is always your own call. Banked tiles are safe for the rest of the game; nothing in this game can ever take a tile back out of a rail.

REFILL. Feel for one tile through night_lid's hand hole for each well that is now empty and set it knob-up into that well without looking at its face. Wells holding a face-up tile are not refilled — face-up tiles stay where they lie until somebody spends a reach on them. If the bowl is empty, empty wells simply stay empty for the rest of the game and the sky thins out.

TURN THE SKY. Rotate exactly one mask disc of your choice by one, two or three index grooves, in either direction. This is compulsory and public. You are not choosing your own sky — you will not read this one — you are choosing the sky the next player must work with, and everyone can see their rail and knows which constellation they are short of. Then move your reach_peg to the socket for four minus the grooves you turned: one groove leaves you three reaches next turn, two grooves leaves you two, three grooves leaves you one. If you busted this turn you must turn exactly one groove, and your peg goes to three.
ADVANCE THE DAWN. Move the dawn_peg one socket along night_bowl's foot flange. This happens every single turn, no matter what anybody did or failed to do. Then play passes clockwise.

end.text: The game ends the instant the dawn_peg leaves the twenty-fourth socket — that is, at the end of the twenty-fourth turn of the game, and no earlier and no later. Nothing on the table can delay it or bring it forward: the discs, the bowl and the wells have no say in the clock. Twenty-four turns divides evenly by two, three and four, so every player has taken exactly the same number of turns however many of you are playing.
Anything not standing in a score_rail when dawn comes is worth nothing: tiles still lying in wells, tiles still in the night_bowl, and every void_tile in the eclipse bay.

win.text: Score your score_rail. Each star_tile standing in it is worth 2 and each moon_tile 1. Then count the tiles in each of your three slots and add 3 points for every COMPLETE NIGHT you have assembled — a complete night is one tile from each of the three constellations, so this is 3 times the number of tiles standing in your shortest slot. Highest total wins. On a tie, the tied player with more tiles in their shortest slot wins; if that ties too, the win is shared.
